Notes for reading

Lesson 1 — Communicating the risk analysis to stakeholders

Report structure, the executive summary, plain language, and the ten-minute briefing · 0:04 – 0:24

1.1 Why the report is part of the analysis

▣ Slide 8 — Why the report is part of the analysis

An analysis that nobody reads changes nothing. The competency of this course, EZ02, lists effective communication with stakeholders among its performance criteria for the whole competency: the analysis is judged by what the readers understand and decide, not by the number of rows in the register.

The frameworks say the same thing. NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) SP (Special Publication) 800-30 Rev. 1VirusTotal treats communicating and sharing the results as a step of the risk assessment in its own right (section 3.3), between conducting the assessment and maintaining it. The Govern function of the NIST CSF (Cybersecurity Framework) 2.0VirusTotal states that the cybersecurity risk management strategy, expectations and policy are established, communicated and monitored. ISO (International Organization for Standardization)/IEC (International Electrotechnical Commission) 27005:2022VirusTotal treats risk communication and consultation as an activity that runs through the whole process, from the first interview to the review of the residual risk.

A risk report is therefore a decision document: it exists so that a named person can approve, fund, assign, accept or refuse something by a date. Every section of the report is written for that purpose.

1.2 Stakeholders: who reads what, and why

▣ Slide 9 — Stakeholders: who reads what, and why▣ Slide 10 — The communication matrix of Kalmia

A stakeholder is a person or an organization that can affect, be affected by, or consider itself affected by a decision or an activity (the definition used by ISO 31000). In a risk analysis the stakeholders are not only the managers: they include the people who carry out the actions, the employees whose daily work changes, and sometimes outside parties such as the managed service provider or the insurer.

For each stakeholder, four questions decide what to send:

  1. What do they decide or do? Approve a budget, carry out an action, follow a new rule.
  2. What must they know to do it? The level of detail follows the task, not the rank: the CEO (chief executive officer) needs the decision and the money; the IT (information technology) coordinator needs the configuration and the evidence.
  3. What must they not receive? Anything they do not need — this is the need-to-know principle of Lesson 2.
  4. In which form, through which channel, and when? One page, a spreadsheet, a briefing, a notice; a restricted share, a meeting, a notice board.

The answers are recorded in a communication matrix: one row per stakeholder, with what they receive, the level of detail, the format and channel, the timing and the classification label. For the decisions themselves, a RACI (responsible, accountable, consulted, informed) matrix names who carries out each action, who is accountable for it (one person only), who is consulted and who is informed.

StakeholderDecides or doesReceivesClassification
Nadia Royapprove the budget, sign exceptions and acceptancesone-page executive summary + 10-minute briefingCONFIDENTIAL
Karim Haddadcarry out and follow his risks' actions; approve change windowshis risks + action plan + change calendarCONFIDENTIAL
Sophie Tremblaybudget lines, insurance, training, offboardingcost table + her risks + training planCONFIDENTIAL
Lucas Martincarry out the technical actions; keep the evidencefull report with the technical annexRESTRICTED
InfoNord (MSP [managed service provider])carry out the actions of its contractextract of the technical annex for its scope only, under the NDA (non-disclosure agreement)RESTRICTED / TLP:AMBER+STRICT
All employeesfollow the new rules (MFA [multi-factor authentication], reporting address)one-page notice: what changes for youINTERNAL

1.3 The structure of a risk analysis report

▣ Slide 11 — Report structure — NIST SP 800-30, Appendix K▣ Slide 12 — The Integrative Project report outline

Appendix K of NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1VirusTotal describes what a risk assessment report contains, in three parts. NIST presents the list as informative and exemplary only: it is a model to adapt, not a mandatory template.

  • Executive summary — the date, the purpose and the scope of the assessment; whether it is a first or a later assessment; the overall level of risk; the number of risks found at each level.
  • Body of the report — the purpose and the questions to answer, the assumptions and constraints, the risk tolerance used, the risk model and the analytic approach, the rationale of the risk-related decisions, the uncertainties and how they influence the decisions, the systems and business functions covered, a summary of the results in tables or graphs, the period for which the assessment stays valid, and the risks from adversarial and non-adversarial threats.
  • Appendices — references and sources, the team and its contact information, and the supporting details and evidence that a reader needs to check or reuse the results.

For the Integrative Project, the same logic gives the outline below. Each part comes from a lab you already completed:

PartContentComes from
Title pagetitle, version, date, classification label, distribution listLesson 2 (tonight)
1 Executive summarydecisions requested, risk today and after the plan, cost, top risks — one pageLesson 1 (tonight), Lab 4 Part F
2 Scope, method and sourcesassets and systems covered, scales, information sources, limits and unknownsClasses 1, 9, 10
3 Assets and threatsasset inventory, infrastructure map, threat catalogueLabs 1 and 2
4 Risk register and prioritiesthe twelve risks, ratings, owners, priority classesLab 3
5 Treatment and prevention plandecisions, controls, cost-benefit, continuity, prevention measuresLab 4 Parts A to E
6 Plan for managementfunded, deferred or transferred measures, change calendar, open decisionsLab 4 Part F, Lesson 3
7 Residual risk and acceptanceresidual register and signed acceptancesLab 4 Part D
Appendicesfull register, technical annex, evidence index, abbreviations, sourcesall labs

1.4 Writing a finding the reader can act on

▣ Slide 13 — Writing a finding — Kalmia's R-01

The body of the report is a series of findings. Auditors write a finding with four elements — the elements of a finding described in the Government Auditing StandardsVirusTotal — and a risk analyst can use the same discipline:

  • Criteria — what should be: a policy, a standard, a contract, a tolerance approved by management.
  • Condition — what is: the fact observed, with its evidence.
  • Cause — why the condition exists: no owner, no procedure, no budget, a default setting.
  • Effect — the consequence for the organization, in time, money, people or obligations.
  • Recommendation — the action that removes the cause, with an owner and a date.

Kalmia's R-01 written as a finding: criteria — the continuity plan of Class 13 requires an off-site, offline copy tested every month (CT-07, linked to the Cyber Centre baseline control on backups); condition — the only backup disk of NAS-01 stays connected to it; cause — no backup procedure and no owner; effect — ransomware would encrypt the shares and the backup together, an outage of about 162 hours against a tolerance of 48; recommendation — CT-07, off-site offline backup with a monthly restore test, owner Karim Haddad, starting in week 1.

A finding without a cause leads to a recommendation that treats the symptom. A finding without an effect leaves the reader asking why it matters.

1.5 The executive summary: the decision comes first

▣ Slide 14 — The executive summary: the decision comes first

Most decision-makers read one page. The executive summary must therefore stand alone: someone who reads nothing else must know what is asked, why, how much it costs and what happens without a decision. Business writers call this order BLUF (bottom line up front): the conclusion and the request come in the first sentences, the explanations after.

Six contents fit on one page:

  1. The decisions requested, each with an owner and a deadline.
  2. The overall risk today and after the plan: the number of risks at each level, and one figure in money (the expected yearly loss).
  3. The three most serious risks in business words: asset, consequence, owner.
  4. The plan and its cost, compared with the approved budget.
  5. A today / after comparison that a manager can picture.
  6. What happens if nothing is done.

The summary carries no IP (Internet Protocol) address, no CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) number, no configuration detail: those belong in the technical annex, for the readers who need them.

1.6 Plain language, numbers and figures

▣ Slide 15 — Plain language, numbers and figures

Plain language is writing that the intended reader understands the first time. The Canada.ca Content Style GuideVirusTotal gives measurable rules: start with the most important information (section 2.2); break up long sentences, the optimum being under 15 to 20 words, with one idea per sentence (section 2.6); and use no jargon or unexplained abbreviation.

Four rules apply to the numbers of a risk report:

  • Every number has a unit and a source: “about $237,700 a year (Lab 3 register, Class 13)”.
  • Round what the reader does not need to the dollar: “about 9 times in 100”, not “8.883 %”.
  • Say when a number is an estimate and how uncertain it is; never present an estimate as a measurement.
  • No alarming words without evidence. Language built to frighten — sometimes called FUD (fear, uncertainty and doubt) — destroys trust the first time a forecast does not happen.

Figures follow one rule: one message per figure, and the title of the figure states the message (“After the plan, no risk stays CRITICAL”). A risk matrix in red, amber and green must also carry the level names or letters, because colour must never be the only means of conveying information (WCAG [Web Content Accessibility Guidelines] 2.2, criterion 1.4.1VirusTotal).

1.7 The ten-minute briefing to management

▣ Slide 16 — The ten-minute briefing to management

A written report is often followed by a short meeting. Ten minutes are enough if the time is planned:

MinutesContentKalmia
0 – 1Purpose and bottom line“Three decisions are needed this week to start the 2027 plan.”
1 – 4The top risks, today and after the plan, with their evidenceR-01, R-02, R-06; 1 CRITICAL and 6 HIGH become 0 CRITICAL and 1 HIGH
4 – 7The plan: what, by whom, when, how much27 controls, $23,710 a year against $20,000
7 – 9The decisions requested, one by oneD1 budget, D2 R-06, D3 acceptances
9 – 10Next steps and the date of the next reportchange calendar from Monday, report in January

Three rules make the briefing work: one slide per message, with the message as the title; the speaker explains the slide instead of reading it; and the briefing ends with the decisions, not with a thank-you slide. After the meeting, the decisions are written in the minutes with their owners and dates, and the register is updated: a risk is treated only when its decision is recorded (Class 12).

1.8 Hard questions and honest answers

▣ Slide 17 — Hard questions, honest answers

Managers ask the same questions in every company. Prepare an answer for each before the meeting:

QuestionWeak answerAnswer that keeps trust
“Are we safe?”“Yes, after the plan.”“After the plan no risk is CRITICAL; one stays HIGH unless you decide D2; nine MEDIUM risks are accepted with your signature.”
“What if we do nothing?”“We will be hacked.”“The expected loss stays about $237,700 a year, and a ransomware outage would last about 162 hours, more than three times the tolerance.”
“Why does it cost more than the budget?”“Security is expensive.”“The full list costs $3,710 more than the budget. Here are two ways to close the gap and what each one leaves open.”
“Can the plan break something?”“No.”“Each change follows CT-39: test, window, rollback. Class 14 listed what each measure can break.”
A question you cannot answera number invented on the spot“I do not know yet; I will send the answer by Wednesday.”

An invented number is discovered sooner or later, and after that every number of the report is doubted. Honesty about the limits of the analysis is not a weakness of the analyst: it is a professional duty (Lesson 2).

1.9 What Kalmia's summary must say

▣ Slide 18 — Kalmia — what the summary must say

The facts of the summary come from the labs: today the register holds 1 CRITICAL, 6 HIGH, 4 MEDIUM and 1 LOW risk; after the plan of Classes 12–13 it holds 0 CRITICAL, 1 HIGH (R-06), 7 MEDIUM and 4 LOW. The expected loss falls from about $237,700 to about $41,954 a year. The full plan costs $23,710 a year against a budget of $20,000, a gap of $3,710. Three decisions are open: the budget (D1), R-06 (D2) and the acceptance records that are ready (D3).

Real-life example 1 turns these facts into the page that Nadia Roy reads on Monday, and Code example 1 checks that page against six writing rules.

Real-life example 1 — Monday 08:30: ten minutes with Nadia Roy

▣ Slide 19 — Real-life example 1 — Monday 08:30

Task. From the Lab 3 register, the plan figures of Classes 13 and 14 and the three open decisions, write the one-page executive summary of Kalmia's 2027 security plan for Nadia Roy, check it against six writing rules, and write the communication matrix that says what each of six stakeholders receives and at which classification.

How it relates. This is Lesson 1 applied: the structure of Appendix K (the executive summary part), BLUF (bottom line up front), plain language and numbers with sources, and the stakeholder questions recorded in a communication matrix.

Labs. Lab 4 — Part F: the one-page summary for Nadia Roy and the open decisions (kalmia_exec_summary.md). Integrative Project report (Class 16, Monday): the executive summary and the distribution list of the title page. Integrative Project presentation (Class 17, Thursday, November 26 — optional, formative): the ten-minute briefing.

On Friday afternoon Nadia Roy sends one line: “Monday 08:30, management meeting. You have ten minutes. What do you need from us?” Lucas Martin exports the register; Sophie Tremblay confirms the cost figures. The team writes the page in the order of BLUF, then checks it.

The summary passes the six rules: 267 words, 16.7 words per sentence on average, no undefined abbreviation, no IP (Internet Protocol) address or CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) number, three decisions with owners and deadlines. Its first paragraph asks for a decision; the method of the analysis is not on the page at all. The communication matrix gives the full report to Lucas Martin only, an extract of the technical annex to InfoNord under the NDA (non-disclosure agreement), and a one-page notice to the employees that says what changes for them and nothing about the weaknesses.

Code example 1 (Python) — kalmia_exec_summary.py

▣ Slide 20 — Code example 1 — kalmia_exec_summary.py

Task. A Python script that reads the register, the plan figures, the decisions and the stakeholders; counts the levels today and after the plan; selects the three most serious risks; writes the executive summary in the BLUF (bottom line up front) order; checks it against six writing rules (decision first, length, sentence length, abbreviations defined, no technical identifiers, owners and deadlines); and writes the communication matrix.

How it relates. Each rule of Lesson 1 becomes a test that the computer can run: the visualization fills the risk matrix of today, compares the levels today and after the plan, shows the budget gap, then ticks the six writing rules and the six rows of the communication matrix.

Run: python3 kalmia_exec_summary.py

  1. The imports bring the modules for CSV (comma-separated values) files, JSON (JavaScript Object Notation), regular expressions and paths; no package needs to be installed.
  2. HERE, DATA and OUT are built from the folder of the script, so the script works from any folder; OUT.mkdir(exist_ok=True) creates the output folder once.
  3. DEFINED lists the abbreviations the summary may use, with their definitions; ALLOWED lists capital words that are not abbreviations (level names, asset names).
  4. band() converts a score into a level with the Kalmia bands (20+ CRITICAL, 10–19 HIGH, 5–9 MEDIUM, 1–4 LOW).
  5. The script reads the register, the plan figures and the decisions; the loop computes each score and level and counts the levels today and after the plan (the residual level of Class 13).
  6. sorted(...)[:3] keeps the three most serious risks: highest score first, then priority class, then identifier; the plan cost and the budget gap follow.
  7. The summary is built line by line in the BLUF order: decisions first, then the levels, the expected loss, the top risks, the today/after comparison, the cost, and the outcome without a decision.
  8. The checks measure the body: words, average sentence length, capital words that are not defined, IP (Internet Protocol) addresses or CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) numbers; each rule prints PASS or FAIL with what was measured.
  9. A last line defines the abbreviations actually used, then the summary, the check results and the communication matrix are written to kalmia_out/.
  10. In this module the runner replays a real recorded run: Start/Pause, Step and Restart move through the 259 recorded steps; click any line of the execution window to see it again with its variables.

The step-by-step runner and the full code are in the lecture page.

finding

Lesson 2 — Professional ethics and confidentiality of analysis results

Codes of ethics, typical dilemmas, classification and TLP labels, need-to-know versions, Law 25 · 0:24 – 0:40

2.1 Why ethics and confidentiality are part of the competency

▣ Slide 24 — Why the results need protection

Two of the performance criteria of EZ02 are about the analyst's conduct: respect for professional ethics and respect for the confidentiality of analysis results. The reason is simple. A risk analysis collects, in one place, the weaknesses of an organization, the paths an attacker could use, the actions that are still open and the dates when they will close. Kalmia's register, its network map and its change calendar together tell a reader where to attack and until when the door stays open.

The analyst also holds the trust of management: Nadia Roy will spend $20,000 on the strength of numbers she cannot check herself. Professional ethics is the set of rules of conduct that a profession expects from its members so that this trust is justified.

2.2 Three codes that apply to you

▣ Slide 25 — Three codes of ethics that apply to you

Three codes of ethics are relevant to a junior analyst in Québec. Their wording differs; their content overlaps.

CodeWhat it asks, in shortWhere
ISC2 (International Information System Security Certification Consortium) Code of EthicsFour canons: protect society and the infrastructure; act honorably, honestly, justly, responsibly and legally; serve employers and clients diligently and competently; advance and protect the profession. Strict adherence is a condition of every ISC2 certification.isc2.org/ethicsVirusTotal
ISACA (Information Systems Audit and Control Association) Code of Professional EthicsSeven principles, among them: work objectively and with due care, keep confidential what you learn and never use it for personal gain, accept only work you are competent to do, and report results honestly with every significant fact.isaca.orgVirusTotal
Course Code of Ethics (Legal Notice s. 9)Ten commitments: act only with authorization; do no harm; respect privacy; keep confidential what you learn, including in labs; be honest; disclose responsibly; respect the law; respect intellectual property; refuse and report unethical requests; take responsibility.Legal Notice v2.0VirusTotal

Codes do not list every situation. They give principles, and the professional applies them with judgment — which is why the next part practises five situations that every analyst meets.

2.3 Five situations that test an analyst

▣ Slide 26 — Five situations that test an analyst
SituationWhat is at stakeWhat the codes requireWhat you do
A manager asks you to lower a rating “because the fix is ordered”the honesty of the reportreport results honestly and completely (ISC2 canon 2, ISACA principle 6, course commitment 5)keep the rating; add “ordered, installation expected on …”; record the request and your answer
The supplier that runs a control provides the evidence that the control worksobjectivitywork impartially; disclose a conflict of interest (ISACA principle 2)accept the evidence as a claim; have an independent person verify it before the rating changes
While reading logs you see personal information that you do not needprivacycollect the minimum, do not look at what you do not need (course commitment 3)stop reading it; do not copy it; quote counts, never records; inform the person in charge of the protection of personal information
A manager asks you to “test” a café neighbour's Wi-Fi or a supplier's portalauthorization and the lawact only with authorization (course commitment 1, Legal Notice s. 6.1); refuse and report (commitment 9)refuse in writing; explain the authorization rule and Criminal Code s. 342.1
You are asked whether a privacy incident must be reported to the regulatorcompetenceaccept only work you are competent to do (ISACA principle 5); Legal Notice s. 16give the facts you know; the decision belongs to the person in charge, with legal advice

A conflict of interest is a situation in which a personal or business interest could influence — or could appear to influence — professional judgment. It is not a fault in itself; hiding it is. The answer is always the same: disclose it in writing and let someone independent check the work.

2.4 A four-step method when you are not sure

▣ Slide 27 — When you are not sure: four steps

When a request feels wrong but you cannot say why, four steps give a defensible answer:

  1. Stop — do not act on the request yet; nothing is lost by taking an hour.
  2. Check — the law, the contract, your written authorization, the policy and the code of ethics. Most questions are answered here.
  3. Record — write down the request, who made it, when, and the facts you know. A record protects you and the organization.
  4. Decide or escalate — if the answer is clear, act and say why; if not, escalate in writing to the person who has the authority (the risk owner, the CEO [chief executive officer], the person in charge of personal information).

The same four steps appear in section 6.8 of the Legal Notice for an accidental discovery: stop, do not disclose, document only what you saw, report to the owner.

2.5 Why analysis results are confidential

▣ Slide 24 — Why the results need protection

The results of a risk analysis contain four kinds of sensitive information:

  • weaknesses and attack paths — what is vulnerable, how it can be reached, which controls are missing;
  • timing — which actions are deferred and until when; an attacker who reads the change calendar knows which door stays open during the holidays;
  • personal information — names in incident reports, account names, sometimes samples of customer data pasted as evidence;
  • business information — costs, contracts, insurance, budget decisions.

Confidentiality of the results means that only the persons who need them for their role receive them, in the version they need, and that the organization can show who received what. Stored and sent copies are encrypted, because their contents are sensitive.

2.6 Classification levels and TLP labels

▣ Slide 28 — Kalmia's four classification levels▣ Slide 29 — TLP 2.0 — how far may it travel?

An information classification scheme gives each document a label and attaches handling rules to the label. Kalmia uses four levels:

Kalmia levelWho may receive itExample tonightHandling
PUBLICApproved for anyonethe public statement on securityno restriction once approved by Nadia Roy
INTERNALAll Kalmia staffthe employee noticeKalmia systems only; not posted outside
CONFIDENTIALNamed managersthe executive summary, the cost table, the action planrestricted share; no personal e-mail; shred printouts
RESTRICTEDNamed persons, need-to-knowthe full report, the technical annex, the registerrestricted share with access log; encrypted copies only; distribution log

When information leaves the organization, a second label tells the recipients how far they may share it. The Traffic Light Protocol (TLP 2.0VirusTotal, published by FIRST [Forum of Incident Response and Security Teams] in August 2022) has five labels:

LabelSharing allowedKalmia example
TLP:REDOnly the individual recipients; no further disclosurea verbal briefing to one person about an ongoing incident
TLP:AMBER+STRICTThe recipient's organization only, on a need-to-know basisthe technical extract sent to InfoNord
TLP:AMBERThe recipient's organization and its clients, on a need-to-know basisa warning that InfoNord may pass to its other clients
TLP:GREENThe recipient's community, not public channelsa lesson learned shared with other Montréal roasters
TLP:CLEARNo limit (copyright rules still apply)the public statement on security

TLP 2.0 renamed the old TLP:WHITE to TLP:CLEAR and added TLP:AMBER+STRICT. The label is written in capitals, without spaces, in the header and the footer of every page. TLP tells the recipient how far to share; it does not replace the organization's own classification and storage rules.

2.7 Need-to-know versions of one report

▣ Slide 30 — One report, five need-to-know versions

Need-to-know means that a person receives only the information required for his or her task — even a senior manager, even a trusted supplier. In practice one master report produces several versions:

VersionSectionsRemovedLabelRecipient
Full reportS1–S5personal informationRESTRICTEDLucas Martin
Management versionS1–S4personal information and technical detailCONFIDENTIALNadia Roy (and the managers)
Technical extractS5 onlypersonal informationRESTRICTED / TLP:AMBER+STRICTInfoNord, under the NDA (non-disclosure agreement)
Employee noticeS6everything except the new rulesINTERNALall employees
Public statementS7everything specificPUBLIC / TLP:CLEARwebsite

Each version is recorded in a distribution list (who must receive it) and a distribution log (who received which version, when, and its fingerprint). Outside parties receive only what their contract covers, under a non-disclosure agreement that obliges them to keep it confidential.

2.8 Redaction, metadata and integrity hashes

▣ Slide 31 — Redaction, metadata and integrity hashes

Redaction removes sensitive data from a copy of a document before it is shared. The data must really be removed, not only hidden: a black rectangle drawn over text in a PDF (Portable Document Format) viewer can leave the text in the file, where anyone can copy or extract it. Redaction by a tool must be followed by a verification of the result — the role of a data loss prevention check, which searches the finished copy for patterns that must not be there.

Metadata — the author, comments, tracked changes, hidden sheets, file properties — travels with the document. Remove it before release.

A cryptographic hash such as SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm with a 256-bit digest) is a fixed-length fingerprint of a file: change one character and the fingerprint changes completely. Recording the hash of each released version in the distribution log lets a recipient check that the file is exactly the one released. A hash proves integrity; it does not hide anything, so it never replaces encryption.

Finally, retention: a report is kept as long as the organization needs it and the law requires, then destroyed securely — shredded printouts, deleted working copies, cleared shares.

2.9 When personal information is involved: Law 25 and PIPEDA

▣ Slide 32 — Personal information: Law 25 and PIPEDA

Kalmia's register contains R-02, the export of 18,500 loyalty records by a former employee's account. Québec's private-sector privacy law, the Act respecting the protection of personal information in the private sectorVirusTotal, as amended by Law 25, applies to that kind of event:

  • A confidentiality incident is any access to, use of or communication of personal information not authorized by law, its loss, or any other breach of its protection (s. 3.6).
  • The enterprise must take reasonable measures to reduce the risk of injury and to prevent new incidents of the same nature (s. 3.5).
  • When an incident presents a risk of serious injury, the enterprise must promptly notify the Commission d'accès à l'informationVirusTotal and the persons concerned; the assessment considers the sensitivity of the information, the anticipated consequences of its use and the likelihood of injurious use.
  • Every incident, serious or not, goes in a register of confidentiality incidents, kept up to date for at least five years and provided to the CAI (Commission d'accès à l'information du Québec) on request.
  • The person in charge of the protection of personal information is, by default, the person with the highest authority in the enterprise — at Kalmia, Nadia Roy — who may delegate the function in writing (s. 3.1).
  • Penalties can reach $10,000,000 or 2 % of worldwide turnover for administrative penalties (s. 90.12), and $25,000,000 or 4 % for penal offences (s. 91).

At the federal level, PIPEDA (Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act)VirusTotal obliges organizations under its authority to report to the OPC (Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada) any breach of security safeguards that creates a real risk of significant harm (RROSH), to notify the individuals, and to keep a record of every breach.

Two consequences for the analyst. First, the report itself must not contain personal information that it does not need: it quotes counts (“18,500 records”), never records. Second, if a report that contains personal information is sent to the wrong person, that mistake is itself a confidentiality incident. This is general course information, not legal advice (Legal Notice s. 8 and 16).

2.10 The rules of this course

▣ Slide 2 — Legal notice — before the examples

Everything above applies to your labs. Section 7.5 of the Legal NoticeVirusTotal keeps any finding about a real organization confidential indefinitely and forbids presenting course work as an audit; section 17 forbids sharing course material, quizzes, labs and solutions; section 18 makes your submitted work your own and confirms that it contains no real personal information. Real-life example 2 — Friday 16:40: two requests and five versions before the plan leaves

▣ Slide 33 — Real-life example 2 — Friday 16:40

Task. Before the plan is released on Friday evening, decide two requests to change a rating — one without evidence, one with evidence produced by the requester itself — then release one version of the report for each of five recipients with the sections they need, the personal information and technical detail removed according to their level, a second verification, a label, and a SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm with a 256-bit digest) hash in the distribution log.

How it relates. This is Lesson 2 applied: honesty of the ratings and conflict of interest (ISC2 [International Information System Security Certification Consortium] canon 2, ISACA [Information Systems Audit and Control Association] principles 2 and 6), need-to-know versions, redaction followed by verification, classification and TLP (Traffic Light Protocol) labels, integrity hashes and the distribution log.

Labs. Lab 4 deliverable Lab4_TeamName_Plan.pdf: the title page carries the classification label, the version and the distribution list; the plan travels only through Léa (Legal Notice s. 17). Integrative Project report (Class 16): the distribution list and the management version. Class 17 presentation: only sanitized slides may be shown to the group.

At 16:40 two messages arrive. Karim Haddad asks to lower R-08 from 12 to 6 because a new disk is ordered. InfoNord asks to lower R-05 from 10 to 4 and attaches its own evidence EV-117. At the same time the five versions of the plan must leave before 18:00.

The verification catches what the automatic redaction missed: the management version contains the account name written in capitals (ADM-LMARTIN), which the case-sensitive rule did not match. The copy is withheld instead of being sent. The fix belongs in the master report — write “the shared administrator account” — after which all five versions pass and the hashes of the two changed copies change too. The customer e-mail and telephone number pasted as evidence EV-104 are removed from every copy; the right correction is to delete them from the master as well, because a report quotes counts, never records.

Code example 2 (Bash) — kalmia_release_report.sh

▣ Slide 34 — Code example 2 — kalmia_release_report.sh

Task. A Bash script that decides the rating-change requests on evidence and flags a conflict of interest; extracts, for each recipient, only the sections that recipient needs; removes personal information and technical detail with sed; verifies each finished copy again with grep (a data loss prevention check) and withholds any copy that fails; and records each release with its SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm with a 256-bit digest) hash in the distribution log.

How it relates. Each rule of Lesson 2 becomes a command: the visualization shows the two requests and their decisions, then fills the matrix of recipients × sections as the copies are built, with the number of redactions, the verification result, the release status and the beginning of each hash.

Run: bash kalmia_release_report.sh

  1. set -euo pipefail stops the script at the first error, on an unset variable or a failing command in a pipe — a safe default for any script that writes files.
  2. HERE, DATA, OUT and REL are built from the folder of the script; rm -rf "$REL" deletes the old release folder so that an outdated copy can never be sent.
  3. The patterns are extended regular expressions: personal e-mail addresses (a dot before the @), the fictional 514-555-01xx numbers, IPv4 (Internet Protocol version 4) addresses with an optional mask or port, the adm- account names and CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) identifiers.
  4. Step 1 reads change_requests.csv with while IFS=, read -r ...: no evidence → REJECTED; evidence produced by the requester → ON HOLD for an independent check; other evidence → TO VERIFY. The rating never changes on a request alone.
  5. extract uses awk to print one section of the master report; redact uses sed to replace the sensitive patterns according to the level (pii or tech); dlp_check searches the finished copy again with grep and prints PASS or the reason for a failure.
  6. Step 2 reads recipients.csv; for each recipient the block between braces writes the header label, the selected sections passed through redact, and the footer label into the copy.
  7. The script counts the redaction markers, runs dlp_check, computes the SHA-256 hash, releases the copy (PASS) or renames it .withheld (FAIL), and appends one line to distribution_log.csv.
  8. The run releases 4 of 5 copies: the management copy is withheld because ADM-LMARTIN (capitals) escaped the redaction but not the case-insensitive check. Correct the master report and run the script again: 5 of 5.
  9. In this module the runner replays a real recorded run (bash xtrace): each step shows the line, its comment, the command after expansion and the variables known at that moment.

The step-by-step runner and the full code are in the lecture page.

Schematic 2 — From one master report to five controlled versions

▣ Slide 35 — Schematic 2 — one master report, five controlled versions

The rating requests are decided first (evidence, conflict of interest). Then each copy passes four gates — need-to-know sections, redaction, verification, label and hash — before it reaches its recipient; a copy that fails the verification is withheld.

Key terms of Lesson 2

▣ Slide 36 — Watch, then check yourself — Lesson 2
professional ethics
the rules of conduct a profession expects from its members so that the trust placed in them is justified
code of ethics
a written set of principles that members of a profession commit to follow (ISC2, ISACA, Legal Notice s. 9)
conflict of interest
a personal or business interest that could influence, or appear to influence, professional judgment; disclose it
need-to-know
each person receives only the information required for his or her task, whatever the rank
information classification
labels (PUBLIC, INTERNAL, CONFIDENTIAL, RESTRICTED) with handling rules attached to each label
Traffic Light Protocol (TLP)
five labels that tell recipients how far they may share: RED, AMBER+STRICT, AMBER, GREEN, CLEAR
redaction
removing sensitive data from a copy before sharing it; the data must be removed, not only hidden
data loss prevention check
a search of the finished copy for patterns that must not leave (personal information, IP [Internet Protocol] addresses, account names)
cryptographic hash (SHA-256)
a fixed-length fingerprint of a file; any change gives a different value; proves integrity, not confidentiality
distribution log
the record of who received which version, when, through which channel, with its hash
confidentiality incident
Law 25: unauthorized access, use or communication of personal information, its loss, or any breach of its protection
person in charge of the protection of personal information
by default the person with the highest authority in the enterprise; may be delegated in writing

Lesson 3 — Priority management: what to fix first and why

Six questions, severity versus priority, BOD 26-04, dependencies, capacity, the freeze and the budget cut line · 0:40 – 0:56

3.1 Why priority management is a competency

▣ Slide 38 — Why priority management is a competency

EZ02 lists effective priority management among its performance criteria. Priority management is the decision about the order in which the actions of a plan are funded and carried out, recorded with the reason for each position. It is needed because four resources are always limited: money (Kalmia: $20,000 a year), people (Lucas Martin works half-time; InfoNord's hours are counted), time windows (changes happen in planned windows, and the web shop is frozen during the holiday peak) and the attention of management.

Kalmia's plan now holds 28 actions. They cannot all start on Monday. The question of this lesson is not “which actions are good?” — they all are — but “which one first, which one later, which one not this year, and why?”

3.2 Six questions, always in the same order

▣ Slide 39 — Six questions, always in the same order

A documented method asks the same questions in the same order, so that another analyst reaches the same result from the same facts:

  1. Is it a must? A legal or contractual duty, a decision already signed, or a precondition of every other change. At Kalmia: CT-39 (the change procedure), and CT-26 as long as R-06 stays HIGH without the CEO (chief executive officer)'s exception.
  2. How urgent is the risk it treats? The priority class of the most urgent risk the action treats: P1 starts within 7 days, P2 within 30 days, P3 within 90 days, P4 at the next review (Kalmia policy, Class 12).
  3. Is it one of the first controls every small organization should have? The Canadian Centre for Cyber Security recommends starting with four: an incident response plan, patching, strong user authentication, and backups with encryption (awareness publication ITSAP.10.035VirusTotal).
  4. How much risk does it remove per dollar? Kalmia's measure: the sum of the scores of the risks it treats, per $1,000 of annual cost. A shared control that treats three risks earns more.
  5. What must come before it? A dependency: CT-21 (camera hardening) needs the camera VLAN (virtual local area network) of CT-09.
  6. Who can do it, when, and with which money? Capacity of the implementer, change windows, the holiday freeze, and the budget cut line.

The reason for the position of each action is written next to it. That record — traceability — lets management check the decision and lets the analyst revise the order when a fact changes.

3.3 Severity is not priority: CVSS, EPSS, KEV and SSVC

▣ Slide 40 — Severity is not priority

For vulnerabilities, four public signals are combined; none of them is a priority on its own.

SignalWhat it measuresLimit
CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System) v4.0VirusTotal (FIRST [Forum of Incident Response and Security Teams])the technical severity of a vulnerability, 0.0 to 10.0it ignores whether attackers use it and how important the asset is
EPSS (Exploit Prediction Scoring System)VirusTotal (FIRST)the probability (0 to 1) that a published CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) sees exploitation activity in the next 30 days; version 4 since March 17, 2025a forecast for the whole Internet, not for your network
CISA (Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency) KEV (Known Exploited Vulnerabilities) catalogVirusTotalevidence that a vulnerability has been exploited in the wildit says nothing about your exposure
SSVC (Stakeholder-Specific Vulnerability Categorization)VirusTotal (CISA and Carnegie Mellon SEI [Software Engineering Institute])a decision — Track, Track*, Attend or Act — from a tree of questions about exploitation, exposure, impact and missionthe tree must be adapted to the organization

Two examples show the difference. A CVSS 9.8 vulnerability on an isolated test computer with no network connection can wait for the normal cycle. A CVSS 7.5 vulnerability listed in the KEV catalog on the Internet-facing web server comes first. NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology)'s guidance on enterprise risk, NIST IR (Interagency or Internal Report) 8286BVirusTotal, makes the same point at a larger scale: risks are ranked by their effect on the objectives of the enterprise, and the priorities and responses are recorded in the risk register.

3.4 A current example: CISA BOD 26-04

▣ Slide 41 — CISA BOD 26-04 — four criteria, five timelines

On June 10, 2026, the US (United States) Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency issued BOD (Binding Operational Directive) 26-04, Prioritizing Security Updates Based on RiskVirusTotal, a directive for US federal civilian agencies. It supersedes and revokes BOD 19-02 and BOD 22-01 — so the two-week rule of BOD 22-01 quoted in older material no longer applies. The directive sets the remediation timeline of a vulnerability from four criteria:

  1. Is the vulnerable asset publicly exposed?
  2. Is the vulnerability in the KEV catalog?
  3. Can an adversary automate the exploitation?
  4. Does exploitation give partial or total control of the asset?

The answers lead to five outcomes: 3 days with a forensic triage for the most dangerous combinations (for example exposed, in the KEV catalog and giving total control), 3 days, 14 days, 60 days, or at the next system upgrade when the asset is not exposed, not in the KEV catalog, not automatable. The table gives every combination (Y = yes, N = no; impact = partial or total control):

Remediation timelineExposed · in KEV · automatable · impact
3 days, with a forensic triageY·Y·Y·total — Y·Y·N·total — N·Y·Y·total
3 daysY·Y·Y·partial — Y·N·Y·total
14 daysY·Y·N·partial — Y·N·Y·partial — Y·N·N·total — N·Y·Y·partial — N·Y·N·total — N·Y·N·partial
60 daysY·N·N·partial — N·N·Y·total — N·N·Y·partial
At the next system upgradeN·N·N·total — N·N·N·partial

CISA explains the idea in Patch Smarter, Not HarderVirusTotal: defer what is low risk, act fast on what is high risk. Kalmia is not bound by the directive, but its own policy follows the same logic with P1 to P4.

3.5 From a ranked list to a calendar

▣ Slide 42 — From a ranked list to a calendar

A ranked list is not yet a plan. Four constraints turn it into a calendar:

  • Dependencies — an action starts only after its prerequisites end, even if it ranks higher (CT-21 waits for CT-09).
  • Capacity — each implementer can carry a limited number of actions at the same time. Kalmia's assumption: Lucas Martin four, InfoNord six, Sophie Tremblay three, Karim Haddad two, the web agency one, Nadia Roy one.
  • Change windows — a change happens in a planned window with a test and a rollback (CT-39; Class 14: Monday 06:00 window, rollback in less than 30 minutes).
  • Freeze periods — Kalmia earns a third of its online revenue in November and December: no change to the web shop or the payment terminals from Friday, November 27 to Monday, January 4, except an emergency change approved by Nadia Roy.

The result is drawn as a Gantt chart: one bar per action, weeks across, the freeze and the deadlines as bands and lines. When an action cannot meet its deadline because of capacity or the freeze, the conflict is not hidden: it becomes an open decision for management — extra hours, an emergency change, or an approved delay.

3.6 The budget cut line

▣ Slide 43 — The budget cut line

Money is allocated in the order of the ranking. Musts and P1 actions are funded first; if they alone exceed the budget, the analyst escalates instead of cutting a P1 action quietly. The other actions are funded while they fit; the first one that no longer fits marks the cut line, and cheaper actions further down can still fit after it.

At Kalmia the musts and P1 actions alone cost $19,820 a year — 99 % of the $20,000 budget. Two management options change the result: a 90-day exception for R-06 (CT-26 waits) or paying CT-33, the replacement of end-of-support computers, from the IT (information technology) equipment budget of about $260,000 a year instead of the security budget. Moving a cost to another budget is a decision for management, not for the analyst.

3.7 Deferral is a decision, not an omission

▣ Slide 44 — Deferral is a decision, not an omission

An action that is not funded or not scheduled this year is deferred. A deferral is valid only if five elements are written down:

  1. the reason (budget, capacity, freeze, dependency);
  2. the compensating control that reduces the same risk meanwhile, if one exists;
  3. the acceptance or exception signed by the right person — at Kalmia, a residual HIGH risk needs the CEO's exception, 90 days at most (Class 13);
  4. an end date or a review date;
  5. a trigger that reopens the decision early — a new incident, a new KEV entry, a change of the asset.

Without these elements a deferred action is simply forgotten, and the register shows a treatment that does not exist.

3.8 Kalmia: the decisions Part F asks for

▣ Slide 45 — Kalmia — the decisions Part F asks for

Real-life example 3 runs the six questions on the 28 actions. With the default rule, 20 actions are funded for $19,970, eight are deferred for $4,540, and two schedule conflicts appear: CT-12 cannot be done before the freeze because the web agency is busy with CT-26, and CT-14 starts one week late because Lucas Martin is fully booked in week 1. The deferral of CT-24 also leaves R-04 without its only corrective control. These are exactly the open decisions that Lab 4, Part F asks you to present to Nadia Roy — with your own choices and reasons.

Real-life example 3 — Saturday 10:00: 28 actions, $20,000 and a holiday freeze

▣ Slide 46 — Real-life example 3 — Saturday 10:00

Task. Rank the 28 actions of the plan (CT-07 to CT-25, CT-32 to CT-39 and the candidate CT-26) with the six questions, draw the budget cut line at $20,000, schedule every funded action in a 14-week change calendar that respects dependencies, the implementers' capacity and the freeze of the web shop and payment terminals, and list the open decisions that the result creates.

How it relates. This is Lesson 3 applied: musts, priority classes, the Cyber Centre's first four controls, value per dollar, dependencies, the budget cut line, capacity, change windows, the freeze, and the conversion of conflicts into decisions for management.

Labs. Lab 4 — Part F: what is funded now, deferred or transferred, with reasons; the change calendar with the P1 actions starting by November 27; the open decisions (kalmia_priority_plan.csv, Gantt chart). Integrative Project report (Class 16): section “Plan for management”.

Saturday morning, Karim Haddad, Sophie Tremblay and Lucas Martin meet with the analyst. The budget is $20,000; the full list costs $23,710, plus $800 for CT-26 if R-06 has no exception. The web shop freeze starts on Friday, November 27.

With the default rule, the musts and the P1 actions use $19,820 of the $20,000; CT-25 and CT-16 still fit, and the first action that no longer fits is CT-18. Eight actions ($4,540) are deferred. Two schedule flags and one deferral become open decisions: CT-12 needs the web agency in week 1 (extra hours, or an emergency change during the freeze), CT-14 starts in week 2 (add capacity or approve the delay), and CT-24 leaves R-04 without its corrective control (fund it, or a dated exception). Tick “CT-33 paid by the IT (information technology) equipment budget” and CT-18, CT-22 and CT-23 are funded too; tick “CEO (chief executive officer) signs a 90-day exception for R-06” and CT-12 moves back to week 1. Neither option is the analyst's to choose: Part F presents them to Nadia Roy with their consequences.

Code example 3 (HTML + JavaScript) — kalmia_priority_planner.html

▣ Slide 47 — Code example 3 — the priority planner

Task. A self-contained web page (no installation, no network) that computes the class, the score sum and the value of each action, sorts the actions with the documented key, checks the dependencies, runs the budget pass, schedules every funded action week by week against the implementers' capacity and the freeze, and writes the open decisions. Its own Start/Pause, Step and Restart buttons play the run step by step in an execution window; three options let you test management decisions; the plan exports to CSV (comma-separated values) and the drawings to SVG (Scalable Vector Graphics) and PNG (Portable Network Graphics).

How it relates. It is Lesson 3 in executable form: panel 1 shows the ranking with the value bars, the decisions and the budget cut line; panel 2 draws the change calendar with the freeze and the deadlines; panel 3 turns the conflicts into the open decisions of Part F.

Run: open kalmia_priority_planner.html in a browser

  1. The data part holds the score and class of each risk, the 28 actions (cost, risks treated, implementer, duration, dependency, freeze tag, first-four flag), the capacity of each implementer, the 14 weeks and the freeze weeks.
  2. buildSteps(opt) computes, for each action, its class (the most urgent risk it treats), its score sum and its value per $1,000, and marks the musts (CT-39, and CT-26 without the R-06 exception).
  3. The sort key is written in one line: must first, then class, then the first four controls (if the option is ticked), then value, then identifier — the six questions in their order.
  4. The dependency check moves a prerequisite before the action that needs it; with Kalmia's data CT-09 already stands before CT-21, and the step says so.
  5. The budget pass funds musts and P1 actions always (and warns if they exceed the budget), funds the others while they fit, defers the rest, and pays CT-33 from the IT (information technology) budget when that option is ticked.
  6. The scheduler looks, for each funded action in rank order, for the first week that ends inside the 14 weeks, avoids the freeze for web shop and payment actions, and leaves a free slot for the implementer in every week of the action.
  7. Each action is checked against its deadline (P1 starts in week 1, P2 ends by week 5, P3 by week 13); a late action gets a flag.
  8. drawRank, drawGantt and drawSummary redraw the three panels for the step reached; the runner (toggle, step, reset) plays the steps with a timer that can be paused and resumed.
  9. The download functions save the plan as CSV and each drawing as SVG or PNG; any change of an option or of the budget prepares a new run.

Key terms of Lesson 3

▣ Slide 49 — Watch, then check yourself — Lesson 3
priority management
deciding the order in which the actions of a plan are funded and carried out, with the reason for each position
priority class
Kalmia's urgency classes: P1 starts within 7 days, P2 within 30, P3 within 90, P4 at the next review
value per $1,000
Kalmia's measure: the sum of the scores of the risks an action treats, divided by its annual cost in thousands of dollars
dependency
a prerequisite: an action that must end before another can start
capacity
the number of actions an implementer can carry at the same time
change freeze
a period in which no change is made to a system, except an approved emergency change
Gantt chart
a calendar with one bar per action from its start to its end, and the deadlines and freezes drawn on it
budget cut line
the point in the ranked list where the next action no longer fits in the budget
deferral
a recorded decision to do an action later: reason, compensating control, acceptance or exception, end date, trigger
severity versus priority
severity (CVSS) describes the vulnerability; priority adds exploitation, exposure, asset importance, cost and dependencies
traceability
the written link between each decision and its reason, so that it can be checked and revised

    The federal rules: report breaches that create a real risk of significant harm, notify individuals, keep a record of every breach.
    https://www.priv.gc.ca/en/privacy-topics/privacy-for-businesses/privacy-breaches-at-your-business/gd_pb_201810/ · Check on VirusTotal

Lesson 3 — Priority management

  • NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) IR (Interagency or Internal Report) 8286B-upd1 — Prioritizing Cybersecurity Risk for Enterprise Risk Management
    February 2025 update: rank cybersecurity risks by their effect on enterprise objectives and record priorities and responses in the risk register.
    https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/ir/8286/b/upd1/final · Check on VirusTotal
  • Canadian Centre for Cyber Security — Baseline cyber security controls for small and medium organizations
    Thirteen control categories for organizations of fewer than 499 employees, built on the 80/20 rule.
    https://www.cyber.gc.ca/en/guidance/baseline-cyber-security-controls-small-and-medium-organizations · Check on VirusTotal
  • Canadian Centre for Cyber Security — Top measures to enhance cyber security for small and medium organizations (ITSAP.10.035)
    Start with four controls: an incident response plan, patching, strong user authentication, backups and encryption.
    https://www.cyber.gc.ca/en/guidance/top-measures-enhance-cyber-security-small-and-medium-organizations-itsap10035 · Check on VirusTotal
  • CIS (Center for Internet Security) Critical Security Controls — Implementation Groups (IG1 [Implementation Group 1])
    IG1, essential cyber hygiene: the 56 safeguards that every enterprise should apply first (CIS Controls v8.1).
    https://www.cisecurity.org/controls/implementation-groups/ig1 · Check on VirusTotal
  • FIRST (Forum of Incident Response and Security Teams) — Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS v4.0)
    The severity score of a vulnerability (0.0 to 10.0). Severity is one input of a priority, not the priority itself.
    https://www.first.org/cvss/ · Check on VirusTotal
  • FIRST (Forum of Incident Response and Security Teams) — Exploit Prediction Scoring System (EPSS)
    The probability (0 to 1) that a published CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) sees exploitation activity in the next 30 days; version 4 since March 17, 2025.
    https://www.first.org/epss/ · Check on VirusTotal
  • CISA (Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency) — Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog
    The authoritative list of vulnerabilities with reliable evidence of exploitation in the wild.
    https://www.cisa.gov/known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog · Check on VirusTotal
  • CISA (Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency) — Stakeholder-Specific Vulnerability Categorization (SSVC)
    A decision tree that ends in Track, Track*, Attend or Act instead of a single score.
    https://www.cisa.gov/ssvc · Check on VirusTotal
  • CISA (Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency) — BOD (Binding Operational Directive) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk (June 10, 2026)
    Four criteria (exposure, KEV [Known Exploited Vulnerabilities] status, exploit automation, technical impact) set remediation timelines from 3 days to the next system upgrade. It supersedes BOD 19-02 and BOD 22-01.
    https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/directives/bod-26-04-prioritizing-security-updates-based-risk · Check on VirusTotal
  • CISA (Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency) — Patch Smarter, Not Harder
    CISA's own explanation of BOD (Binding Operational Directive) 26-04: defer lower-priority vulnerabilities and focus on the highest risk.
    https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/news/patch-smarter-not-harder · Check on VirusTotal
